doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

title: What he listens for and working with engineers
summary: His recording values, collaboration with Jim Anderson and Chris Vescera, and tape editing with a razor blade.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Do you think your — how do I describe — what you listened for changed as your role expanded?

What I listened for? No my values stayed the same. And they were established very early in my listening habits. I like mono and simple stereo recording. The multi-track recording I have no problem with it. Digital recording I have no problem with it. But all I’m really interested in is what ends up on those two tracks.
Did you ever have any disagreements with engineers?

Not much. Occasionally. I’m pretty direct about what I want to do. I had like really good engineers that liked my playing, you know I had worked a lot with Jim Anderson, the great engineer that recently is teaching at NYU, the Tisch School. In fact he started their own recording program there 25 years ago or something and he was the engineer for “Jazz Alive” which was based in DC. And they recorded Phil’s group live several times and I really liked what he did and I liked him. We became friends and I had a friend in Pennsylvania that ran a little — was the engineer at a little studio called Mountain Sound. His name was Christopher Vescera. Chris Vescera. And he eventually moved out west and he’s still out there. He’s been out west for 40 years now but in the beginning he helped me put together those two LPs. Because I had the tapes but you know I needed editing and we had to do a couple of interesting things that — you don’t really talk about

what you do so much because people think they know things and most of them don’t. But you know, you have to use my understanding of the music and the technology in editing and so forth. You know we used to cut tape with a razor blade.
I recall the first time I saw that I was stunned that such a thing was possible.

I didn’t know until I first did a session or something and I saw the engineer do it and then put it back together and like wow. I remember he used to listen, he would turn the reels and he’d listen for the bass drum [scats] to hit the spot.
Yeah. Well I got really good at that. Both those guys were great but I also worked with — well you work with any engineer who is competent and there are plenty of those.
